sectors.name: Literature
sectors.intro: From the slave narrative of Olaudah Equiano (1789) and the first novels in Igbo, Yoruba and Hausa, to Achebe, Soyinka and today's prize-winning generation, Nigerian prose is one of the most read and studied literatures in the world.

timeline.t: Olaudah Equiano publishes The Interesting Narrative in London, one of the earliest books by a writer of Nigerian (Igbo) origin.
Pita Nwana's Omenuko, the first major novel in the Igbo language.

D. O. Fagunwa's Ògbójú Ọdẹ nínú Igbó Irúnmalẹ̀, the first full-length novel in Yoruba.
Amos Tutuola's The Palm-Wine Drinkard is published by Faber and Faber in London.
Cyprian Ekwensi's People of the City, an early urban Nigerian novel in English.
Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart — the most widely read African novel, translated into dozens of languages.
Heinemann's African Writers Series launches with Achebe as founding editor.
Flora Nwapa's Efuru — the first internationally published novel in English by a Nigerian woman.
Wole Soyinka becomes the first African to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
Ben Okri wins the Booker Prize for The Famished Road.
NLNG establishes the Nigeria Prize for Literature.
Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie wins the Orange Prize for Half of a Yellow Sun.
Chigozie Obioma's The Fishermen is shortlisted for the Booker Prize (again in 2019 for An Orchestra of Minorities).
Olubunmi Familoni wins the Nigeria Prize for Literature (children's literature) for The Road Does Not End.
Oyin Olugbile wins the $100,000 Nigeria Prize for Literature with her debut novel Sanya.

sectors.name: Music
sectors.short: Musicians, from talking drums to Afrobeats
sectors.intro: Court drumming, griot and praise-singing traditions gave way to palm-wine, jùjú and highlife in the early 20th century, Fela's Afrobeat in the 1970s, fújì, and the global Afrobeats movement that now fills stadiums and wins Grammys.

timeline.t: Talking drums (dùndún, gángan), bàtá, Hausa court music (maroka praise-singers) and Igbo ogene traditions anchor music in royal, religious and community life.
Jùjú emerges in Lagos, with Tunde King among its pioneers.
Highlife era: Bobby Benson, Victor Olaiya and Rex Lawson dominate the dance halls.
Fela Kuti and Tony Allen create Afrobeat; Kalakuta Republic becomes a centre of music and protest.
King Sunny Adé releases Juju Music on Island Records, taking jùjú to world audiences.
Babatunde Olatunji shares the first Grammy won by a Nigerian-born musician (Planet Drum).
2Face Idibia's African Queen becomes a continental hit, a landmark for Nigerian pop.
The Headies (then Hip Hop World Awards) hold their first edition.
Wizkid features on Drake's One Dance, a Billboard Hot 100 No. 1.
Burna Boy (Twice as Tall) and Wizkid (Brown Skin Girl) win Grammys on the same night.
Rema's Calm Down peaks at No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100; Tems wins a Grammy for Wait For U; Burna Boy headlines London Stadium and Citi Field.
Tems wins Best African Music Performance at the Grammys (Love Me JeJe); Nigerian artists earn over ₦60bn on Spotify.
Davido, Burna Boy, Ayra Starr and Wizkid are all nominated for the Grammy for Best African Music Performance.

sectors.name: Film & TV
sectors.intro: From the first film screening at Lagos' Glover Memorial Hall in 1903, through the Yoruba travelling-theatre films of the 1970s and the home-video boom sparked by Living in Bondage (1992), Nollywood has become one of the world's most prolific film industries.

Behind the Scenes passes ₦2bn; Nollywood out-earns Hollywood in West African cinemas for the first time.
My Father's Shadow (Akinola Davies Jr.) wins Best Movie and Best Director at the AMVCAs.

sectors.name: Journalism
sectors.short: Journalists, editors, broadcasters and the press
sectors.intro: Nigeria's press began with Iwe Irohin in Abeokuta in 1859, was a weapon of the independence struggle, survived decrees and assassinations under military rule, and today spans newspapers, broadcast and award-winning investigative newsrooms.

stats.label: Journalists killed since 1992
stats.note: At least 12 confirmed killed for their work (CPJ, Aug 2023)

timeline.t: Iwe Irohin, the first newspaper in Nigeria, is published in Yoruba in Abeokuta.
The Anglo-African, the first newspaper in Lagos, is launched.
The Daily Times of Nigeria begins publication.
Nnamdi Azikiwe founds the West African Pilot, a voice of the nationalist movement.
WNTV in Ibadan becomes the first television station in Africa.
Decree No. 4 criminalises 'false' reporting; Newswatch magazine is founded.
Newswatch editor Dele Giwa is killed by a parcel bomb.
Under military rule, TELL and TheNEWS practise 'guerrilla journalism'.
Dele Olojede wins the Pulitzer Prize for International Reporting.
The Freedom of Information Act is signed into law.
BBC Africa Eye's Sex for Grades investigation, with Kiki Mordi, exposes harassment in universities.

sectors.intro: From blogs in the mid-2000s to Instagram skits, YouTube channels and TikTok lives, Nigerian creators have built audiences in the tens of millions and a fast-growing creator economy. Follower counts here are refreshed by a weekly bot from official sources.

timeline.t: Linda Ikeji starts her blog, which grows into one of Nigeria's most-read entertainment sites.
Mark Angel Comedy launches on YouTube.
Mark Angel Comedy becomes the first African YouTube channel with 1 million subscribers.
The #EndSARS protests are organised and amplified largely on social media.
The federal government suspends Twitter in Nigeria (June 2021 – January 2022).
Hilda Baci sets a Guinness World Record for the longest cooking marathon by an individual, watched live by millions online.
TikTok reaches an estimated 47.8m Nigerian adults, ahead of every other platform.
